{"id": "3:79/q31", "question": "Which Christian beliefs are discussed as the verse's target?", "turns_on": "Which elements of Christian sonship and Trinity are shared or sect-specific.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q31/p1", "position": "Christian claims about Jesus", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538: The opening denies the belief that Jesus should be worshipped. RAZI-FULL, d. 606: After describing scriptural scholars' distortion, Razi says one altered claim was that Jesus asserted divinity and commanded people to worship him; the verse refutes that charge. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685: The verse denies and rebuts the claim that Jesus is a deity to be worshipped. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885: After establishing attributes of Jesus that exclude divinity, the passage now comprehensively denies that Jesus or any human like him called people to worship him, which by itself refutes their claim. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885: The denial applies to every person who shares Jesus's description, including Ezra and others, rather than addressing Jesus alone. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270: Another view treats the verse as a denial and refutation directed at those who worship Jesus. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: The qualifier apart from God stigmatizes the demand to worship the speaker: servitude cannot be divided, so Christians who make Jesus lord and God's son have abandoned God's worship despite claiming both allegiances. TABATABAI, d. 1402: These verses form a second argument defending Jesus from Christian claims: he is neither God nor someone who claimed divinity, since he is a created human, born and raised by his mother, though fatherless like Adam. | mentions 3:59 ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412: Jesus's deification by later followers exemplifies arbitrary interpretation; the surah presents Mary, Jesus, and Zachariah and stresses Jesus's humanity, mortality, and call to worship God alone. | mentions 3:79 STUDYQURAN citing most commentators: Most commentators connect the verse to Islam’s rejection of Jesus’ worship; it also condemns other worship of humans, as in 9:31. | mentions 9:31 STUDYQURAN: The verse is thematically related to 5:116, where Jesus denies telling people to take him and his mother as gods apart from God. | mentions 5:116"}, {"id": "3:79/q31/p2", "position": "Claims of Jesus's divine sonship and Trinity", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Christians diverged into more than seventy broad sectarian positions, with many finer disputes among them. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النصارى: The Qur'an reports the claim that God is one of three. | mentions 5:73 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an tells Christians to stop saying three. | mentions 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an focuses on what Christians say about Jesus and his mother because those claims touch monotheism. | mentions 9:30, 21:26, 5:72, 5:73, 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an gives less attention to related details such as textual corruption and redemption. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads Qur'an 43:86, Jesus's witness, and Qur'an 4:159 and 5:110 as supporting Jesus's intercession. | mentions 43:86, 4:159, 5:110 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The account of Jesus's testimony at judgment neither establishes nor denies intercession; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains why its wording does not make either case. | mentions 5:116, 5:117, 5:118, 5:119 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Christian redemption by substitution is distinct from intercession and would negate God's absolute sovereignty. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النصارى: The Qur'an reports Christians saying that the Messiah is God's son. | mentions 9:30 TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النصارى: The Qur'an also cites the claim that the Merciful has taken a son. | mentions 21:26 TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النصارى: The Qur'an reports the claim that God is the Messiah, son of Mary. | mentions 5:72"}, {"id": "3:79/q31/p3", "position": "Christian sectarian accounts of sonship", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing الملكانية: The Melkites held that Jesus was God's son in a literal sense. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النسطورية: The Nestorians described descent and sonship as light shining on a transparent body like crystal. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing اليعقوبية: The Jacobites held that God transformed into flesh and blood. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Though Christian schools differ, the Qur'an targets their common claim of Jesus's divine sonship and the related doctrine of Trinity. | mentions 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The uniform Qur'anic argument shows that it addresses the shared doctrine rather than each sect's detailed formulation. | mentions 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Torah and present Gospels affirm one God, while the Gospel also states sonship and identifies the son with the Father. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Christians did not read Gospel sonship as merely honorific, even though some passages explicitly use it that way."}, {"id": "3:79/q31/p4", "position": "Three hypostases in one substance", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Christian doctrine described here preserves Jesus as God's son while affirming one God: one substance has three hypostases, existence (Father), knowledge or Word (Son), and life (Holy Spirit); the Word descends with the Spirit. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats the Qur'an's several descriptions of Christian belief as one shared doctrine: unity understood through Trinity, the common element across the sects. | mentions 9:30, 5:72, 5:73, 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Ordinary generation divides material substance and gradually raises a new member of the same kind, so it entails materiality and developmental processes incompatible with God."}, {"id": "3:79/q31/p5", "position": "Gospel language of sonship", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Gospel passages apply the language of Father and children to Jesus's followers as well, supporting an honorific sense in some contexts. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Other Gospel declarations present Jesus as the way to the Father, as one in the Father, and as having come from God; together with the Word passage, these appear to affirm more than honorific sonship."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q32", "question": "How is divine sonship or incarnation rejected?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, referents, readings, or explanations for this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q32/p1", "position": "Creation and dependence rule out divine offspring", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Because every being depends on God, no independently existing being could match him as an equal offspring; divine generation would also imply gradual action under matter, motion, and time. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads Qur'an 2:116–117 as separate proofs: God is exalted above offspring, all creation belongs to and obeys him, and he originates creation and brings commands to be immediately. | mentions 2:116, 2:117 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Alternatively, “Originator of the heavens and earth” itself rules out generation because God creates without a prior model, whereas a child would reproduce its parent's likeness. | mentions 2:117 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Even if Christians mean a nonmaterial, non-temporal separation by sonship, father and son still entail real plurality: a dependent son is not God, while an independent equal would violate monotheism. | mentions 4:171"}, {"id": "3:79/q32/p2", "position": "Jesus's worship and obedience rule out divinity", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus's worship of God proves that he is a servant rather than God; the angels' worship similarly shows they are not divine daughters, and the Holy Spirit is not God. | mentions 4:172, 21:26, 21:27, 21:28 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Gospels portray the Holy Spirit as obeying God and his messengers, which is incompatible with the Spirit being God commanding or obeying itself. | mentions 21:26, 21:27, 21:28 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus calls the Israelites to worship God as his Lord and theirs; the Gospels likewise report that he acknowledged God as his Lord and never explicitly called people to worship himself. | mentions 5:72 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Because Jesus never explicitly invited worship of himself, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī interprets the Gospel saying “I and my Father are one” as meaning that obeying Jesus is obeying God. | mentions 4:80"}, {"id": "3:79/q32/p3", "position": "Jesus's human origin rules out divinity", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Qur'an 4:171 states the general argument that God is one and has no offspring. | mentions 4:171 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus's gestation, birth, nursing, growth, aging, and ordinary bodily conditions show that he lived as a natural human and therefore was created like other people. | mentions 5:73, 5:75 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Miracles and Jesus's birth without a father are extraordinary but possible events, not evidence of divinity; Adam and prophets also had miraculous origins or deeds without becoming divine. | mentions 5:73, 5:75"}, {"id": "3:79/q32/p4", "position": "Jesus's bodily needs rule out divinity", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an singles out eating because it clearly proves materiality and need: hunger and thirst relieved by food and drink show dependence incompatible with divine self-sufficiency. | mentions 5:75 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus's human conditions were real, not appearance or imagination; the Gospels repeatedly call him human and recount ordinary bodily needs, so he could be harmed or killed like others. | mentions 5:17, 5:76 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an's questions about who could prevent God from killing Jesus and his mother, and whether they can control harm or benefit, reinforce that Jesus is subject to God's dominion. | mentions 5:17, 5:76"}, {"id": "3:79/q32/p5", "position": "Divine sonship is impossible", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an refutes Trinity by two routes: generally, showing that divine sonship is impossible; specifically, showing that Jesus is a created servant rather than God's son."}]}

oved by a substitute, and whether that leaves moral law effective.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q33/p1", "position": "Ransom defeats law and moral responsibility", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an calls human beings needy and God self-sufficient, whose nature excludes need, defect, abasement, or humiliation. | mentions 35:15 TABATABAI, d. 1402: If union makes God literally cursed, it entails the stated impossibility; if the curse is figurative, another's suffering cannot make God himself the ransom. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The atonement claim shows that its proponents misunderstand sin, its connection to afterlife punishment, and its relation to religious law. TABATABAI, d. 1402: In ordinary human society, laws are conventional rules designed to protect communal interests, with punishment serving as deterrence. | mentions 2:26, 2:213 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Qur'anic teaching goes further: obedience and disobedience form real inner virtues or vices that become afterlife bliss or torment, with Paradise and Hell representing nearness to or distance from God. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Divine law completes God's creative guidance: it supports sound social life and afterlife happiness through law and worship that purify the person and bring divine honor. TABATABAI, d. 1402: If Adam's one sin doomed him and his descendants absent Christ's ransom, legislation before Christ could not help; Abraham, Moses, and earlier righteous people would have died saved or damned without a meaningful role for their laws. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The only way to explain pre-ransom legislation would be that God knowingly concealed its futility and misled people while hoping to solve the problem later. TABATABAI, d. 1402: If ransom brings mercy to all without regard to belief or deeds, religious teaching and good works after it have no purpose. TABATABAI, d. 1402: If ransom helps only believers in Christ, almost all people remain damned, including earlier prophets; this conflicts with the Gospels' affirmation of Torah and its mission. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The claim that earlier scriptures promised Christ is speculative before Moses, and a promise of salvation is not an instruction to believe in or worship Christ. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Appealing to a prophecy does not cure the uselessness of moral and practical law, including Christ's own teachings in the Gospels. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The doctrine still makes God's purpose of extending mercy and happiness to all fail, since all but a small group face eternal punishment."}, {"id": "3:79/q33/p2", "position": "Inherited guilt is unjust and forgivable", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing المسيح: The Gospels depict Jesus as making monotheism and love of God the first commandments. | mentions 12:108 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī's aim is to show how the Christian account conflicts with Qur'anic teaching, then distinguish Qur'anic intercession from Christian redemption. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an speaks in terms near human understanding so people can distinguish truth from falsehood, good from evil, and benefit from harm. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Adam's tree prohibition was guidance for his welfare, not a legislative command; its breach brought loss of paradise and nearness, not afterlife punishment. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an and rational proof exonerate prophets from committing sins or violating God's command. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an says God forgave Adam; reason likewise rejects the idea that guilt is ineradicable, since forgiveness removes sin's effects. | mentions 20:122, 2:37 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Inherited guilt would punish people for another's deed, which the Qur'an denies and reason deems unjust. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an denies that one person bears another's sin, a principle reason supports because punishing the innocent is unjust. | mentions 53:38, 53:39 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an distinguishes major sins from lesser ones and says sins below polytheism may be forgiven; polytheism requires repentance for forgiveness. | mentions 4:31, 4:116 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Reason rejects treating every sin alike: a slap differs from murder, and eating from the tree does not merit eternal punishment like disbelief. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Christian solution to a supposed conflict between mercy and justice assumes a humanlike God governed by external interests and liable to error, ignorance, and change. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Such a being would be material, bodily, created, and human rather than the necessary Creator."}, {"id": "3:79/q33/p3", "position": "Divine sovereignty excludes ransom", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: God gives every created thing its form and guides it to its end; this universal guidance includes religious guidance for human beings. | mentions 20:50 TABATABAI, d. 1402: God's first religious guidance to Adam and his companions promised safety to followers and lasting punishment to rejecters, summarizing later legislation with its promises and warnings. | mentions 2:38, 2:39 TABATABAI, d. 1402: God neither wavers from nor reverses a settled decree; the cited verses say he does not forget, faces no superior obstruction, and carries out his purpose. | mentions 38:84, 50:29, 12:21, 65:3, 20:52 TABATABAI, d. 1402: God created and legislated purposefully, then repays each person according to deeds without being overruled by a partner, ransom, friendship, or unauthorized intercession; ransom itself is substitution to transfer harm from the liable person. | mentions 40:17 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Ransom is a transaction that transfers the right and authority over the liable person to a substitute, thereby sparing the liable person from harm. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Divine sovereignty is real and cannot be transferred; unlike human legal sovereignty, which is conventional and alterable, all things and their effects exist through God. TABATABAI, d. 1402: God explicitly rules out ransom on the Day of Judgment. | mentions 57:15 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus says his only role among people was the divinely assigned mission of conveying the message and witnessing their deeds while he remained with them. | mentions 5:116, 5:117 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus leaves their punishment and forgiveness entirely to God, which rules out ransom because he claims no power or connection to release them from divine punishment. | mentions 5:117, 5:118"}, {"id": "3:79/q33/p4", "position": "Incarnation and curse are incoherent", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an and decisive reason affirm God's absolute perfection and immutability, excluding bodily form and human frailties; the Two Testaments attribute such traits to God. | mentions 37:159 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Incarnation cannot unite the necessary, timeless, spaceless God with a human body that develops from embryo to fetus, whatever Christian group’s account of the union. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Paul's attacks on philosophy and reason serve propagation and preaching strategy, as the context of his letters shows. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Given their portrayal of God as prone to error, claiming divine immunity from mistakes is incoherent; rebellion is inapplicable to God, so divine impeccability is also inapplicable. TABATABAI, d. 1402: If God can become human, he could become any species or several at once and perform incompatible acts or bear contradictory attributes. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He questions the claim that Christ bore crucifixion and a curse because the crucified are cursed, asking what such a curse means."}, {"id": "3:79/q33/p5", "position": "Christian inherited sin and redemption claim", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing النصارى: Christians teach that Adam's sin and its inheritance left humanity facing eternal punishment; Christ, both divine and human and sinless, incarnated through Mary and accepted cursed crucifixion as ransom for believers and the whole world. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says crucifixion and redemption form the core of Christian preaching, while the Qur'an makes monotheism the foundation of Islam's call. | mentions 12:108"}]}
{"id": "3:79/q34", "question": "How does intercession differ from ransom?", "turns_on": "Whether another acts by God's permission or substitutes for divine sovereignty.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q34/p1", "position": "Intercession preserves divine sovereignty", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The denied compensation in 2:48, the sale in 2:254, and protection from God in 40:33 each describe something akin to ransom, so their denial rejects ransom. | mentions 2:48, 2:254, 40:33 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The Qur'an presents Jesus's intercession in place of the ransom doctrine attributed to Christians. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Intercession arises from the intercessor's nearness and standing with God; it neither gives the intercessor ownership over God nor cancels God's rule or the law of requital. | mentions 2:48 TABATABAI, d. 1402: Intercession is a prayer asking God to exercise a permissible act of his own dominion, such as forgiving someone whom he has the right to punish. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Ransom is instead a transaction that transfers sovereignty from the one holding a person to the thing paid as ransom, releasing the person from the holder's control. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Qur'an 43:86 permits intercession by those who witness the truth knowingly; Jesus qualifies because God taught him scripture and wisdom and calls him a witness on Judgment Day. | mentions 43:86, 3:48, 5:117, 4:159"}, {"id": "3:79/q34/p2", "position": "Jesus can intercede", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī recalls the claim that Jesus is among those who intercede and whose intercession is accepted."}]}

{"id": "3:79/q37", "question": "What history of Christianity is recounted?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, referents, readings, or explanations for this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q37/p1", "position": "Alternative account of Jesus and early preaching", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jewish religious leaders opposed Jesus and accused him to Pilate of teaching that just, compassionate non-Jews could stand equal before God to scripture readers. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Pilate chose to seize and imprison Jesus to keep the crowd from killing him in its tumult. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Pilate could not establish the reason for the accusations: people shouted labels such as unbeliever, heretic, and traitor without explaining the case. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus told Pilate that he sought no political power, valued spiritual life above bodily life, urged kindness, and worshipped the one God as Father of living creatures. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Experienced in Stoic and other Greek philosophy, Pilate found no fault in Jesus' account and again resolved to save him from the Jews. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jewish leaders spread that Pilate had been deceived by Jesus and was betraying Caesar, seeking his removal amid earlier unrest in Palestine. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Because imperial forces were weak and officials were expected to avoid public complaints, Pilate yielded to the crowd's demand for Jesus' execution as a public-order measure. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Jesus faced death without fear, forgave the Jews who caused it, and was crucified while people mocked and insulted him. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing جلاديوس أنسا: Ansa says Yusuf recounted Jesus' story to him while weeping. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He says trinity, incarnation, and a divine being's suffering as ransom were known among ancient peoples across Asia, Egypt, Persia, and the West. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing دوان: Duan says the most famous Hindu theological worship was the trimurti: Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva as three inseparable forms of one god. TABATABAI, d. 1402: In Ansa's account, Yusuf refused a gold gift and told him to give it to someone poorer. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Yusuf knew little about Paul beyond that he was a tentmaker who left his trade to preach a new faith in a merciful, compassionate God, unlike the Jewish image of Yahweh. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The account says Paul first traveled to Asia Minor and then Greece, teaching slaves that they were all children of a loving Father. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Paul's message, as summarized here, made shared happiness available to poor and rich who lived in brotherhood, purity, and friendship. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī infers that the cited account presents Christianity after Jesus as a prophetic mission from God, not God appearing in human form and redeeming people through atonement. TABATABAI, d. 1402: After the crucifixion, Jesus' disciples and later adherents, including Paul, spread Christianity in India, Africa, Rome, and other lands. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Christian groups disagreed over Christ's divinity, whether faith in him replaced Mosaic law, and whether the Gospel superseded or supplemented Torah. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author argues that peoples first reached by Christian preaching already held pagan, mystical, or Brahmanical ideas of divine incarnation and trinity, including sacrificial redemption."}, {"id": "3:79/q37/p2", "position": "Missionary spread and rational disputes", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says Christian preachers rejected rational argument because critics demanded reasoned grounds, and instead appealed to mystical disclosure and fullness of the Holy Spirit, like Sufis claiming a way beyond reason. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says church scholarship weakened itself by treating Father, Son, Spirit, crucifixion, and atonement as unquestionable premises; a sound superstructure cannot repair a weak foundation. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He argues that trinity and atonement are irrational, and rejects the defense that impossible doctrines should be accepted as religious mysteries. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Missionaries became ascetics and traveled widely, as recounted in Acts and historical works. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Their success, especially in Rome, came partly from widespread injustice, enslavement, and sharp divisions between rulers

TABATABAI, d. 1402: After the Ottomans captured Constantinople and killed its last emperor, Russian rulers claimed succession to church leadership through family ties; Russia's church remained outside Rome. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says that after the last Russian tsar and his family were killed by communists in 1918, the Church of Rome nearly returned to its pre-schism position. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Another group left Rome's church and authority over Gospel teaching; the author calls them Protestants. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author explains that this history is included to help readers trace historical changes and possible pagan influence on Christian doctrine through inheritance, transmission, mixture, or habit. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says treating rationally impossible teachings as axioms caused early Christian disputes in Rome, Alexandria, and other schools. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The church tried to enforce doctrinal unity by convening councils for new teachings and condemning, exiling, expelling, or killing those who remained unconvinced. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing أريوس: Arius taught that the Son was not equal to the Father, that God alone was eternal, and that Christ was created. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says the Council of Nicaea met under Constantine with 313 bishops and adopted a creed calling Jesus uncreated true God, incarnate, crucified, risen, and returning to judge, alongside belief in the Holy Spirit, one baptism, church, resurrection, and eternal life. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The church later convened many councils to reject groups including Nestorians, Jacobites, Arians, and other named doctrinal movements. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The church gradually brought most European peoples and kingdoms into Christianity; the account says Russia converted near the end of the fifth century, in 496. TABATABAI, d. 1402: As northern invasions and wars weakened emperors, Roman subjects handed temporal as well as religious rule to the church, combining both powers in Pope Gregory in 590."}, {"id": "3:79/q37/p5", "position": "Modern aftermath of Pauline Christianity", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī traces Christian pagan doctrines to excessive exaltation of Jesus, culminating in Trinity, crucifixion and atonement, and the sufficiency of belief over works. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Christian practice first bound followers to the church through fasting, prayer, and baptism; secular law and materialism later weakened religious teaching and eroded morals. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He says communism and socialism, built on dialectical materialism, reject divinity, fixed moral virtues, and religious acts, leaving a materialistic, animalized humanity. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He characterizes recent religious revivals as political performances used by politicians to pursue their aims. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing جوزف شيتلر: Schittler says America's new religious revival applies religion to modern civic life to show that modern civilization does not oppose religion, risking complacency about possessing the true faith. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing جورج فلوروفسكي: Florovsky calls American religious instruction a false comfort; a living, genuine revival would have to rest on deep, realistic instruction. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He concludes that the movement began by restoring belief, morals, virtues, and religious law but ended by replacing all with sensual enjoyment, a development from Paul's original deviation. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He argues that present civilization, which threatens humanity, would more credibly be called Pauline civilization than civilization led by Christ."}, {"id": "3:79/q37/p6", "position": "Medieval Christian polemics against Muslims", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author recounts stories that a pope made a German emperor stand barefoot outside his palace in winter for three days and kicked a king's crown when he knelt for pardon. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The author says crusading Christians depicted Muslims as idolaters to rally followers, claiming they worshipped three named gods and sometimes two more, and that Muhammad claimed divinity or had a golden idol. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The reported Christian polemic names Mahum, Ilīn, and Tarphagan as Muslim gods, sometimes adds Martuan and Jupin, and attributes a golden idol to Muhammad. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing ريشار: Richard's poem urges the Franks to throw Mahumand and Tarphagan into fire as an offering to their God. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing رولان: The Song of Roland portrays Mahum as a huge, finely crafted gold-and-silver idol on an elephant, jeweled and glittering. TABATABAI, d. 1402: A poem claims Muslims' gods came to help in battle; after a Muslim defeat, a commander sent for Muhammad from Mecca, and a crowd brought him amid music and dancing while his caliph awaited and worshipped him. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing ريشار: Richard's poem says sorcerers put a jinn inside the idol Mahum, where it first roared and then spoke to listening Muslims."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q38", "question": "How should scripture and transmitted reports be interpreted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q38/p1", "position": "Reasoned exegesis beyond transmission", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: A warning against interpretation should prompt careful reflection and reject haste; scholars differ in this, and some carry scrupulous caution to excess. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: If transmission means early material from Ibn Abbas’s and Ibn Masud’s students, successors’ unattributed, differing interpretations still show they reasoned independently, as seen in al-Tabari and similar works. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing الطبري: Although al-Tabari sets out to restrict himself to Companion and Successor reports, he repeatedly selects and prefers interpretations using evidence from Arabic, thus going beyond that limit. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing بقي بن مخلد: Baqi ibn Makhlad preceded al-Tabari’s approach, though Ibn Ashur says his tafsir has not been seen; Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim followed a similar path. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: Ibn Ashur praises exegetes who did not confine themselves to transmitted material: al-Farra and Abu Ubayda, then al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani, and later al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing الأصمعي: Al-Asma'i refused to explain Quranic vocabulary: he would not say أسرى and سرى or أعصفت and عصفت were equivalent, nor add to his heard definition of خليل as pure, firm affection. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: Ibn Ashur says that outside the fundamentals of belief, God requires reasoned probability supported by evidence, with suitable evidence varying by subject; the principles of understanding speech are known. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: Ibn Ashur rejects the slogan that Quran interpretation must be confined to transmitted material because its advocates have not defined what counts as transmitted. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: If transmission means only sound or fair Prophetic explanations, the restriction narrows Quranic meanings, contradicts their own tafsirs, and falsely implies early Muslim imams limited themselves to Prophetic reports. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing عمر بن الخطاب: Umar asked learned people about the meanings of many verses without requiring them to cite a Prophetic explanation. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: If transmission includes only the Prophet and Companions, as al-Suyuti’s al-Durr al-Manthur appears to do, the material remains too scant to sustain tafsir. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing علي بن أبي طالب: Ibn Ashur says little tafsir is transmitted from most Companions; reports from Ali vary in soundness, and Ali said he had no extra

{"id": "3:79/q39", "question": "How does the argument continue in 3:80?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, referents, readings, or explanations for this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q39/p1", "position": "Continuation concerning angels and prophets", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538: A subjunctive reading of ولا يأمركم is coordinated with the preceding construction; in أيأمركم, the subject may be the human or God, and the interrogative hamza expresses denial. BURHAN, d. 794 citing بعضهم: One analysis takes لا as genuine negation and supplies an omitted coordinated clause, understood as and that they believe. BURHAN, d. 794: With يأمركم in the accusative, one view coordinates it with يؤتيه and treats لا as extra, reinforcing the earlier negation. BURHAN, d. 794 citing بعضهم: Another view coordinates يأمركم with يقول: one given scripture would not call people to worship him and then order worship of angels and prophets. BURHAN, d. 794: A further view says لا is not extra: Muhammad forbade Quraysh and the People of the Book from worshipping angels, ʿUzayr, or Jesus. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing الجمهور: The majority read يأمركم in the nominative as a fresh clause; restarting negation after لكن makes the sense clear: a human neither tells people to worship him nor commands angel worship. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing ابن عامر، وحمزة ويعقوب، وخلف: Ibn Amir, Hamza, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read يأمركم in the accusative, coordinating it with أن يقول; لا is emphatic, since making it governed by أن would reverse the intended meaning. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: One occasion report says the Prophet warned Quraysh against worshipping angels, Jews against Uzayr, and Christians against Jesus; they asked whether he wanted them to take him as lord, prompting revelation."}, {"id": "3:79/q39/p2", "position": "Continuation to verses 81–83", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538: The passage continues with the beginning of verses 81–83 of Al ʿImran. | mentions 3:81, 3:82, 3:83"}, {"id": "3:79/q39/p3", "position": "Variant reading of 3:80", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing الدوري عن أبي عمرو: Al-Duri from Abu Amr gives the reading with a weakened, near-silent damma."}, {"id": "3:79/q39/p4", "position": "Shift to direct address in 3:80", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: The clause and he does not command you shifts from third-person reference to direct address."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q40", "question": "What limits claims made about prophetic revelation?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, referents, readings, or explanations for this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q40/p1", "position": "Aisha rejects claims of sight, concealment, and unseen knowledge", "reasons": "TIRMIDHI citing عائشة: Masruq reports that ʿĀʾisha named three grave lies: that Muhammad saw God (she identifies the figure as Gabriel, seen in his created form only twice), concealed revelation, or knew the unseen; she cites revelation against each claim. | mentions 6:103, 42:51, 53:13, 81:23, 5:67, 27:65 TIRMIDHI citing أبو عيسى: Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih."}, {"id": "3:79/q40/p2", "position": "True report agrees with Book and Sunna", "reasons": "TUSTARI: True report agrees with Book and Sunna (as recorded by TUSTARI)."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q01", "question": "How does this rebuke connect to the preceding covenant and sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the link is the covenant, preceding signs, universal submission, or prophetic authority.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q01/p1", "position": "It follows the covenant to affirm Muhammad and exposes rejecting scripturalists as seeking another religion despite the evidence.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 3:81 and says envy and hostility explain refusal, as with Iblīs; al-Bursawī says the covenant was in their scriptures. Al-Biqāʿī links 3:18–19, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī the one religion and later messengers, and al-Sāmarrāʾī 3:85."}, {"id": "3:83/q01/p2", "position": "The sequence follows the prior signs and turns their force into a fresh question.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, and al-Ṭabrisī say fāʾ adds sequence that wāw lacks; Abū Ḥayyān sees the link to 3:82."}, {"id": "3:83/q01/p3", "position": "Universal submission supplies the argument that people should seek Islam, the religion suited to human nature.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this clause gives the cause in place of its conclusion."}, {"id": "3:83/q01/p4", "position": "Resistance to God's messengers is untenable because no one can evade His grasp.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī notes that miracles establish messengership, so defiance of the messenger defies his sender."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q02", "question": "How are the opening hamza and fāʾ construed?", "turns_on": "Whether fāʾ connects directly, follows an omitted question, or the opening is rendered assertively.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q02/p1", "position": "The hamza introduces rebuke while fāʾ coordinates the question with the preceding statement or result.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Nasafī connect it to prior transgressors; al-Rāzī says the verb is questioned. Al-Samīn notes the hamza's precedence. Al-Ālūsī permits coordination with the combined condition and result or result alone and prefers direct linkage where ellipsis is unnatural."}, {"id": "3:83/q02/p2", "position": "An omitted question, 'Do they turn away?', precedes the fāʾ and the seeking question.", "reasons": "Sibawayh and most grammarians supply it; Ibn Hishām calls it primary. Al-Shams ibn al-Ṣāʾigh defends comparable ellipsis in 13:33; al-Ālūsī accepts it when natural."}, {"id": "3:83/q02/p3", "position": "It can also be translated as the assertion that they seek another religion.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports al-Rāzī's rendering, but says either form marks the futility of turning away."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q03", "question": "Why is 'other than God's religion' placed before 'seek'?", "turns_on": "Whether fronting focuses the false object or simply uses an allowable order while rebuking the act.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q03/p1", "position": "The object is fronted to focus denial and rebuke on seeking a false religion.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ālūsī focus on the object. Al-Biqāʿī and al-Itqān say this does not entail exclusive seeking; interpreting it as 'only another religion' misplaces the rebuke."}, {"id": "3:83/q03/p2", "position": "Denial concerns the act of seeking; fronting is syntactic latitude and resembles the verse's cadence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's rationale; al-Samīn questions the Shaykh's account, and al-Ālūsī dismisses Abū Ḥayyān's explanation."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q04", "question": "What is the grammatical role of 'other than'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q04/p1", "position": "Ghayra is the accusative object of 'seek'.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī give this parse."}]}

{"id": "3:83/q06", "question": "What does 'seek' mean, and why do these people seek elsewhere?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is the word's sense, sustained practice, or the motives and figurative scope.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q06/p1", "position": "Yabghūn means seek or pursue; here it describes following or practicing another religion.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says 'seeking' implies sustained practice; al-Jishumī traces baghy to seeking and unjust striving for superiority.
